title: The Mu'tazilah
hook: the theologians who stepped aside, and kept thinking about justice
tomorrow: The trial of the created Qur'an

segments.voice: Yesterday, kalam, speaking about Allah with arguments, and your line: faith seeks understanding. Did your one deep question stay with you? Today, a school that pushed reason hard. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

A mosque in Basra, in Iraq. The teacher al-Hasan al-Basri sits with his students, and someone asks a hard question. A Muslim commits a grave sin. Is he still a believer, or has he left the faith? Before the teacher can answer, one student, Wasil ibn Ata, offers a third answer: neither. A place in between. Then he gets up, moves to another pillar, and some of the others go with him. That, at least, is the story people tell about how a group got its name: the Mu'tazilah, those who withdraw. Today, the people who stepped aside and kept thinking.
screen: `A HARD QUESTION IN BASRA.` → `A THIRD ANSWER.` → `THOSE WHO WITHDRAW.`

segments.voice: The Mu'tazilah were theologians who treated reason as a gift from Allah: a way to understand revelation, not a way around it. They're remembered as calling themselves the people of justice and oneness, so take those two in turn. Justice first. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! Allah wrongeth not even of the weight of an ant." The Mu'tazilah took that line all the way. If Allah is just, they argued, He does not punish people for what they could not help. So human beings must truly choose their own acts. Reward and punishment only make sense if the choice is really ours. Then oneness. They guarded tawhid so closely that they grew wary of anything eternal standing beside Allah. That led to the claim they're remembered for: the Qur'an is Allah's speech, and it was created, brought into being by Him. To their ears, an uncreated Qur'an sounded like a second eternal thing next to God. Their opponents heard it the other way around. The Qur'an, they said, is Allah's own speech, and His speech is not a made thing like a chair or a mountain. That disagreement didn't stay in the classroom. Tomorrow it becomes a trial. And here is why the Mu'tazilah still come up in conversations about Islam. Their question doesn't age. If God is just, what does that say about my choices? Later theologians, Sunni and Shia, answered it in different ways, and some of them we'll meet later in this part. But the question, sharpened in Basra, is still on the table.
screen: `REASON AS A GIFT, NOT A RIVAL.` · `JUSTICE: ALLAH WRONGS NO ONE.` · `ONENESS: NOTHING ETERNAL BESIDE HIM.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION THAT DOESN'T AGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about justice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small unfairness from this week, something you saw, or something you did. Keep it small. Don't solve it, and don't judge anyone. Just ask the Mu'tazili question quietly: what would a just response look like here? Let a picture of fairness form, even a blurry one. If you pray, you can recall the line: Allah wrongeth not even of the weight of an ant. If you don't, the plain question is enough. The bell holds the time.
The Mu'tazilah. Those who withdraw: theologians of reason who stressed Allah's justice and oneness, and said the Qur'an was created. Today's word.

Your line: justice and reason. Today, when something strikes you as unfair, look for the reason before you reach the verdict. Tomorrow, the trial of the created Qur'an. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Students of Islamic theology study the Mu'tazilah as an early school of kalam that stressed Allah's justice and oneness, held that humans truly choose their acts, and taught that the Qur'an was created.

fork.setup: you're a student in Basra. someone asks: is a Muslim who commits a grave sin still a believer? what do you say?
fork.reveal: in the story people tell, Wasil ibn Ata gave the third answer, then moved to another pillar, and the group got its name: those who withdraw.

original.note: Arabic: those who withdraw, or stand apart.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Mu'tazilah were people who put reason above faith.
what it means: theologians who used reason to defend Allah's justice and oneness, and said the Qur'an was created.
what a scholar hears: the people of justice and oneness, and an origin story about a student who moved to another pillar.
